newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Enterprise profit up, quashes bid talk.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Enterprise profit up, quashes bid talk.

text.p: Shares in Enterprise Oil Plc rose on Thursday after Britain's biggest independent exploration and production firm reported a profit and dividend increase, raised its output estimate and quashed recent bid rumours.
Profit after tax rose 40 percent to 142.5 million pounds ($228.8 million) from 101.6 million due to higher crude oil prices and increased production.
Last year's earnings were actually lower than most analysts had forecast, but the stock market was pleased the dividend was raised by a penny to 17.0 pence.
Enterprise additionally boosted investor confidence by saying it expected its 1999 production to be 320,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day (boepd) rather than the 300,000 previously forecast.
Recent discoveries in the UK in particular prompted Enterprise to review its output estimate.
The company is active in Britain, Denmark, Italy and Norway, while it is also working hard to make the Gulf of Mexico a new core area.
Average output in 1996 rose three percent to 242,932 boepd.
Shares in Enterprise, which were last year's best performing FTSE 100 blue chip stock on the London exchange, rose 23-1/2 pence to 657 in late morning trade.

Several other shares in the oil sector fell as Enterprise's new chief executive, Belgian-born Pierre Jungels, poured cold water on recent market rumours that Enterprise was preparing itself for a major acquisition.
Bid hopes had flared up following a weekend press report, saying Enterprise might make an acquisition this year of up to one billion pounds.
Monument Oil and Gas Plc was mentioned as a potential target as was British-Borneo, which also has promising operations in the Gulf of Mexico.
But Jungels said Enterprise was not interested in either firm and said that chances of an acquisition in 1996 were no bigger than in previous years.
British-Borneo consequently fell 20 pence to 1,402-1/2, while Monument retreated three pence to 82-3/4.
Jungels, meanwhile, sang the praises of Enterprise's high quality and low risk assets, which would enable the firm to consistently repeat its solid performance in the last two years.

Jungels, who took over the helm from current chairman Graham Hearne in January, said Enterprise had an advantage over many rivals in that it was not plagued by political unrest or major environmental headaches in the countries where it operates.
The company also had the benefit of being only slightly involved in natural gas, where persistent oversupply has depressed prices, said Jungels, who used to be a British Gas executive.
"Enterprise has a high quality asset base because in comparison to a lot of competitors we are mostly in oil and in safe countries," he said.
The combination of good assets and highly skilled staff is "the guarantee that we can reproduce the performance of the past two years on a consistent basis," Jungels said.
